This is not legal advice regarding cases that will likely be litigated for years. I was not there, I am not privy to all the details, and many relevant facts have not been disclosed despite the investigation.

You asked, so I will answer. National backorders and shortages may have contributed to the decision not to use the hyperbaric bupivacaine commonly included in standard spinal trays. Duration of action and an ERAS or rapid discharge protocol may also have favored the off label use of mepivacaine MPF as the neuraxial anesthetic in these cases rather than and an FDA approved for spinal anesthesia preparation of bupivacaine. 

What does not make sense to me is the separate decision to have the pharmacy batch the medication. If the selected local anesthetic was already available in a preservative free formulation at the intended concentration and baricity and required no dilution or additives, there was little justification for having a pharmacy technician transfer this inexpensive local anesthetic from its original vial into syringes for multiple patients. Lots of caveats there.

That transfer removed the administering clinician’s ability to inspect the source vial and converted a potential one preparation error potentially harming one patient into a multipatient exposure. The physician anesthesiologist or nurse anesthetist could have drawn the medication directly from the manufacturer’s original vial immediately before administration and personally verified the drug, concentration, lot number, and expiration date.

There are legitimate arguments against my position. Medication substitution errors do occur, and independent verification by a second person generally helps reduce those errors.

I encourage you to read the following report which does go into detail on the defined errors that occurred specifically within the pharmacy in the Ascension cases. 

I was disappointed that the year of the hire date of the pharmacy techs was redacted from the report. 

United States, Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Statement of Deficiencies and Plan of Correction: Ascension Saint Thomas Hospital. CMS Form 2567, survey completed 21 Aug. 2026. Read the CMS report.
https://www.wkrn.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/73/2026/08/Ascension_Saint_Thomas_Hospital_2567_reviewed_8262026_R.pdf.

TMA III Update

For those who do not live and breathe NSA/IDR, the QPA #QualifyingPaymentAmount is essentially an insurer calculated median contracted rate that is one factor in out of network payment disputes.

The key determinations of the 5th Circuit:

The court generally supported the Eastern District Court’s Findings.   Insurers cannot use “ghost rates”contractual rates for services a physician/provider never actually furnished to calculate the QPA. This includes nominal placeholder rates such as $1.

Insurers cannot categorically exclude bonuses, incentives, risk-sharing adjustments, and other payment adjustments attributable to the service when determining the statutory “total maximum payment.”

The court did allow insurers to continue excluding genuine one off single case agreements from QPA calculations.

Importantly, the Fifth Circuit affirmed vacatur of the unlawful federal QPA provisions and rejected the government’s argument that vacating them would be too disruptive.

The mandate has not yet issued, and current federal enforcement discretion guidance remains important during the transition, so this should not be interpreted as an instruction to immediately change current billing/IDR operations.

For physicians, however, this is a major legal victory because the Fifth Circuit has now expressly rejected QPA methodologies capable of incorporating artificially low payment rates.

Today I testified before @TexasTDI on proposed Network Adequacy Rulemaking (Docket 2868).

Health plans often argue they cannot find physicians or facilities willing to contract. Yet our June 2026 review of nearly 50,000 network adequacy waivers requested across all 254 Texas counties revealed several important patterns.

Most striking: 36% of all waivers originated from just 10 of Texas’ most populated counties, not rural Texas.

If plans cannot build adequate networks in Harris, Dallas, Tarrant, Bexar, Collin, Denton, Travis, Montgomery, Williamson, and El Paso Counties areas with some of the highest concentrations of physicians, healthcare professionals, and facilities in Texas the answer is not weaker rules.

The answer is transparency, accountability, and enforcement of HB 3359.

Texans pay for PPO and EPO coverage expecting real access to in-network care.

In a U.S. Department of Justice @TheJusticeDept case involving ketamine tied to the death of Matthew Perry, Dr. Salvador Plasencia, physician, was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison and fined approximately $5,600; Dr. Mark Chavez, physician, was sentenced to 8 months of home confinement and 300 hours of community service; and today Jasveen Sangha, “the Ketamine Queen,” a non-physician ketamine distributor, was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison.

As a physician and anesthesiologist, my perspective is clear: ketamine is a powerful anesthetic medication. Regardless of the indication, it should be administered in a safe, monitored healthcare environment with a physician immediately available to manage potential complications such as respiratory depression, cardiovascular effects, or other serious reactions. We must learn from the #opioidcrisis and avoid a #ketaminecrisis

🪡 🧵I appreciate @EdGainesIII bringing up the healthplans priorities & refuting them. I will expand on his discussion.
1/ AHIP claims it wants to “make health care more affordable.” https://www.ahip.org/news/articles/five-steps-congress-can-take-to-make-health-care-more-affordable
As a solo independent physician who deals daily with the No Surprises Act (NSA) and IDR, here’s a fact-based, point-by-point response using backing claims— not talking points. 

AHIP’s July 30, 2025 article claims Congress should “Stop Private Equity’s Misuse of the No Surprises Act (NSA).” I’m a solo independent physician who works daily inside NSA Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR), and the real problem is health plans’ “No / Low / Slow Pay” after they LOSE binding arbitration, combined with procedural gamesmanship that forces small practices like mine to keep writing obscene checks just to get paid fairly.

CMS reports that as of Nov. 30, 2025, 4,634,956 IDR disputes had been initiated and over 3.2 million payment determinations issued.
https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/policies-and-resources/reports

Congressional Research Service reports ~$718 million in IDR fees in 2024 alone, with initiating parties’ offers selected ~85% of the time, which directly contradicts the claim that physicians  are abusing arbitration.
https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R48738/R48738.2.pdf

The AMA documents that late payment & nonpayment after IDR determinations is widespread, despite the statute requiring timely payment.
https://www.ama-assn.org/health-care-advocacy/access-care/one-wrinkle-surprise-billing-law-health-plans-aren-t-paying

Mixed court decisions on enforcement of NSA IDR determinations is a Red Line that Congress needs to Act to eliminate judicial ambiguity. 
https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-ctd-3_24-cv-00680/pdf/USCOURTS-ctd-3_24-cv-00680-1.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com

https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/24/24-10561-CV0.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com
